title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbooks, and Benchmarking Suite
author: Ava Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling model, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on the serving runtime, SRE, and performance-focused reviewers who run and maintain Redwood Inference's GPU-backed inference clusters.

Goals
- Provide a single reference for architecture decisions and operational procedures.
- Standardize profiling and benchmarking to ensure reproducible performance regressions and optimizations.
- Document known issues and mitigations to speed incident response.

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

High-level components:
- Frontend API router: request validation, auth, rate limiting, route-level SLO checks.
- Smart router: policy engine that routes to hosted/dedicated/private pools or model variants based on latency/cost/region.
- Execution fleet: GPU nodes running the inference engine (continuous-batching, KV cache management, quantization profiles).
- Orchestration service: placements, autoscaler, and maintenance windows.
- Observability pipeline: per-token tracing, aggregated latency/cost metrics, logs, and sample outputs for eval monitoring.

Key interfaces and contracts:
- Model artifacts: ONNX/FlashAttention-compatible artifacts with quantization metadata in model.manifest.json.
- Request contract: JSON RPC over HTTP with fields {model, prompt, max_tokens, stream, trace_id}.
- Cache contract: prefix-keyed KV cache with TTL and invalidation policy.

SLOs and targets (examples)
- SLO (short generations, <= 128 tokens): p50 < 20ms, p95 < 80ms, p99 < 250ms.
- Throughput target (per-GPU, 8xA100-like equiv): 4000 tokens/sec for batched short requests.
- Error budget: 0.1% errors per hour per route before paging SRE on-call.

Ownership and lifecycle
- Owners: serving-runtime core team (primary), eng-sre (secondary).
- Model onboarding owner: applied-ml-and-evals.
- Release cadence: weekly runtime builds; quarterly major upgrades for kernels/compilation stacks.

2) Kernel scheduling and placement policy

Design summary:
- Purpose: maximize token throughput while maintaining latency SLOs by selecting kernel variants and packing inference work onto available SMs.
- Two-layer selection: 1) Kernel candidate selection by model architecture and sequence-length profile. 2) Scheduling policy that decides per-GPU packing (co-locate small low-latency jobs with long-running high-throughput jobs when safe).

Scheduling heuristics and rules:
- Priority and preemption: latency-sensitive routes have priority token reservation. When contended, best-effort jobs yield via cooperative preemption (KV checkpoint + context switch).
- Packing heuristics: greedy-fit by estimated peak memory + conservative headroom (10%) to avoid OOM due to allocator fragmentation.
- Kernel variant selection: prefer fused kernels for decoder-only models when sequence < 512; use tiled kernels for very long sequences.
- Fallbacks: if chosen kernel OOMs, auto-fallback to lower-memory kernel and emit event to perf-monitoring.

Configuration table (example)
- model_type: decoder-only | encoder-decoder
- preferred_kernel: fused | tiled | memory-optimized
- sequence_threshold: numeric (tokens)
- reserved_headroom_pct: numeric (default 10)

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile a regression)

When you observe a suspected regression in latency/throughput or a performance PR:
1. Verify the signal
   1) Confirm with metrics: check p50/p95/p99 token latency, token/sec, and GPU utilization over the incident window.
   2) Correlate with release IDs and model versions.
2. Reproduce locally (recommended environment)
   - Use the perf-runner image: ghcr.io/redwood/perf-runner:stable
   - Commands (example):
     - ./perf-runner --model ./artifacts/my-model --batch-sizes 1,2,4 --seq-lens 32,128,512 --tokens 10000 --report out.json
   - Reproduce at same quantization profile and kernel flag set.
3. Capture traces and profiler outputs
   - NVPROF/Nsight wrappers are available on debug nodes: /usr/local/bin/runtime-nsight-wrap --duration 60 --output trace.nvprof
   - Runtime internal trace: curl -H 'X-Debug:trace' 'https://runtime.local/debug/trace?trace_id=<id>' > trace.json
4. Analyze outputs
   - Look for kernel timings, memory allocator stalls, cross-device memcpy, and cudaLaunch latencies.
   - Verify whether p99 spikes align with GC-like events or kernel fallback paths.
5. Mitigate or revert
   - If regression introduced by kernel change, pin kernel selection to previous variant and run canary.
   - Create a rollback PR and coordinate with releases.

Profiling checklist (short)
- [ ] Confirm metric alert and time-range
- [ ] Reproduce with perf-runner at target quantization
- [ ] Collect GPU traces + runtime traces
- [ ] Compare before/after artifacts and kernel sets
- [ ] File an incident or regression ticket with artifacts and stack traces

4) Benchmarking suite (guidelines, test matrix, reproducibility)

Purpose: ensure we measure unit economics (tokens/sec, latency) and regressions across model variants, sequence lengths, and batching patterns.

Test matrix (recommended)
- Models: small (1B), medium (7B), large (70B) representative artifacts
- Sequence lengths: 32, 128, 512, 2048
- Batch sizes: single request (1), interactive (1-4), batched (8, 16, 32)
- Quantization profiles: fp16, int8, q4_0

Bench reproducibility steps
1. Use the canonical benchmark environment: perf-bench-2026 image tag.
2. Lock kernel/compilation flags via BENCH_FLAGS env. Example: export BENCH_FLAGS='--kernel=fused --allocator=jemalloc --cuda-launch-ms=1'
3. Run the benchmark harness and store artifacts: ./run-bench.sh --model my-model --out /bench-results/my-model-20260921.json
4. Record environment details in bench metadata: CUDA driver, GPU model, docker image, git commit hash.

Reporting and dashboards
- Bench results are uploaded to the perf dashboard (internal) with metadata and diffs against the baseline (last green run).
- Any >3% regression on p95 or >5% regression on tokens/sec for a production model must open a regression ticket and block kernel-level releases until triage.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)
- 2026-09-14: Introduced memory-optimized kernel for decoder-only models which reduced OOMs by 60% on mixed workloads.
- 2026-07-01: Added automated fallback path for tiled kernels to improve stability on longer sequences.
- 2026-06-01: Upgraded allocator to jemalloc-5.3 with improved fragmentation behavior.

6) Known issues and mitigations
- Pinned allocator fragmentation in mixed small/large request workloads: mitigation: reserved_headroom_pct increased to 15% on affected pools.
- Occasional p99 spike when KV cache invalidations coincide with large-batch compactions: mitigation: stagger invalidation windows and add lockless compaction path.
- Intermittent CUDA driver compatibility causing kernel launch failures on certain 2024-era images: mitigation: upgrade node images to driver 525+ and pin driver in release bundles.

7) Runtime runbooks (incident playbooks)

A. High p99 latency for short generations (pager)
1. Triage (5 min)
   - Confirm alert details (routes affected, time window).
   - Collect recent deploys and kernel change list (git tags) in last 2 hours.
2. Immediate steps (10 min)
   - If a kernel change deployed in the last 60 minutes, rollback kernel variant via feature flag and monitor.
   - If no recent changes, reduce autoscaler burst to give headroom to latency-sensitive pools.
3. Deeper investigation (30-90 min)
   - Run perf-runner against affected model with production flags.
   - Attach nsight traces and check for blocking memcpy or allocator stalls.
4. Post-incident
   - Create postmortem with root cause, action items, and regression test to prevent recurrence.

B. GPU OOMs on serviced pool
1. Triage
   - Identify job and recent artifact changes.
   - Fetch GPU metrics (memory usage timeline) and kernel selection events.
2. Mitigation
   - Immediately drain the node if repeated OOMs and move workloads to safe pools.
   - Increase reserved_headroom_pct to 20% for the pool and restart pods.
3. Long-term
   - Add a bench case that exercises worst-case memory fragmentation and include in pre-merge checks.

8) Team wiki and references
- Runtime team repo: git.internal/redwood/serving-runtime (owner: Ava Chen)
- Perf dashboard: https://internal.perf.redwood/dashboard (owner: eng-platform)
- Profiling utilities: /usr/local/bin/runtime-nsight-wrap and gs://redwood-perf/tools/perf-runner
- On-call roster: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations

Contact and escalation

Notes
- Keep all benchmark runs reproducible and attached to PRs that modify kernels, allocators, or scheduling logic.
- This doc is a living reference; update the runbooks after each major incident with concrete examples and artifacts.
